title: Theorem
body_md:
(1) Let $\Gamma$ be any given graph in Figure 1, which is given as $\Gamma_p$ or 
$\Gamma_{p,i}$. Assume $W_\Gamma$ is a strong symplectic filling of the contact plumbed manifold $(Y_\Gamma,\xi_{LM})$. We consider the following conditions on $W_\Gamma$.
\begin{itemize}
\item [{(i)}] There is a surjective homomorphism $\bar{\rho}: \pi_1(W_\Gamma)\rightarrow {\mathbb Z}_p$ extending the homomorphism $\rho: \pi_1(Y_\Gamma)\rightarrow {\mathbb Z}_p$, i.e., $\rho=\bar{\rho}\circ i_\ast$ where $i_\ast: \pi_1(Y_\Gamma)\rightarrow \pi_1(W_\Gamma)$. Let $\tilde{W}_\Gamma\rightarrow W_\Gamma$ be the $p$-fold covering associated to $\bar{\rho}: \pi_1(W_\Gamma)\rightarrow {\mathbb Z}_p$. Note that $\tilde{W}_\Gamma$ is a strong symplectic filling of 
$(\tilde{Y}_\Gamma,\tilde{\xi}_{LM})$.
\item [{(ii)}] $H_1(W_\Gamma,{\mathbb Q})=0$ and $i_\ast: H_2(Y_\Gamma,{\mathbb Q})\rightarrow H_2(W_\Gamma,{\mathbb Q})$ is an isomorphism. 
\item [{(iii)}] $H_1(\tilde{W}_\Gamma,{\mathbb Q})=0$.
\item [{(iv)}] The image of the kernel of $i_\ast: \pi_1(\tilde{Y}_\Gamma)\rightarrow  \pi_1(\tilde{P}_\Gamma)$ under $i_\ast: \pi_1(\tilde{Y}_\Gamma)\rightarrow  \pi_1(\tilde{W}_\Gamma)$
normally generates $\pi_1(\tilde{W}_\Gamma)$ and the kernel of $i_\ast: \pi_1(\tilde{Y}_\Gamma)\rightarrow  \pi_1(\tilde{W}_\Gamma)$ maps onto $\pi_1(\tilde{P}_\Gamma)$ under $i_\ast: \pi_1(\tilde{Y}_\Gamma)\rightarrow  \pi_1(\tilde{P}_\Gamma)$.
\end{itemize}
If $W_\Gamma$ obeys (i) and (ii), then the symplectic $4$-manifold $M_\Gamma:=
\tilde{W}_\Gamma\cup_{(\tilde{Y}_\Gamma,\tilde{\xi}_{LM})} \tilde{P}_\Gamma$, which comes equipped with a pseudofree symplectic ${\mathbb Z}_p$-action, having $W_\Gamma\cup_{(Y_\Gamma,\xi_{LM})} \overline{P}_\Gamma$ as the symplectic quotient orbifold, is of a positive canonical class, with Euler characteristic $\chi(M_\Gamma)=3$ and signature $Sign(M_\Gamma)=1$. In particular, 
$M_\Gamma$ is a $4$-manifold on the Bogomolov-Miyaoka-Yau line. Furthermore, $M_\Gamma$ is a 
${\mathbb Q}$-homology ${\mathbb C}{\mathbb P}^2$ if and only if (iii) is obeyed, and $M_\Gamma$ is an exotic ${\mathbb C}{\mathbb P}^2$ if and only if both (iii) and (iv) are obeyed. 

(2) Conversely, suppose there is a symplectic ${\mathbb Q}$-homology ${\mathbb C}{\mathbb P}^2$ with positive canonical class, denoted by $M$, which admits a pseudofree symplectic ${\mathbb Z}_p$-action for an odd prime $p$. Then there is a weighted graph $\Gamma$
in Figure 1, where $\Gamma=\Gamma_p$ or $\Gamma_{p,i}$ for some $i$, such that the corresponding contact plumbed manifold $(Y_\Gamma,\xi_{LM})$ admits a strong symplectic filling $W_\Gamma$ obeying (i)-(iii), and $M$ can be identified with the $4$-manifold $M_\Gamma$. Moreover, if $M$ is an exotic ${\mathbb C}{\mathbb P}^2$, then (iv) is also obeyed by $W_\Gamma$.

title: Remark
body_md:
Theorem 1.1 offers a potential construction of a symplectic exotic ${\mathbb C}{\mathbb P}^2$; indeed, if there is a weighted graph $\Gamma$ in Figure 1, such that the corresponding contact plumbed manifold 
$(Y_\Gamma,\xi_{LM})$ admits a strong symplectic filling $W_\Gamma$ obeying (i)-(iv) (e.g., $W_\Gamma$ obeys (i)-(ii) where $\bar{\rho}: \pi_1(W_\Gamma)\rightarrow {\mathbb Z}_p$ is isomorphic, cf. Corollary 4.6), then the corresponding $4$-manifold $M_\Gamma$ is a symplectic exotic ${\mathbb C}{\mathbb P}^2$. On the other hand, a symplectic ${\mathbb Z}_p$-action of prime order on an exotic ${\mathbb C}{\mathbb P}^2$ must be pseudofree with $p>2$ (cf. \cite{C}, Section 4). It follows easily that Theorem 1.1 also offers a possible nonexistence proof, i.e., if one can show that for any of the graphs $\Gamma$ in Figure 1, $(Y_\Gamma,\xi_{LM})$
does not admit any strong symplectic fillings obeying (i)-(iv), then there is no symplectic exotic 
${\mathbb C}{\mathbb P}^2$ with a nontrivial finite order symplectomorphism.

title: Theorem
body_md:
Let $(M,\omega)$ be a ${\mathbb Q}$-homology ${\mathbb C}{\mathbb P}^2$ with $c_1(K)\cdot [\omega]>0$, where $K$ denotes the canonical line bundle of $(M,\omega)$, such that $M$ is equipped with a pseudofree smooth ${\mathbb Z}_p$-action preserving the symplectic structure $\omega$, where $p>2$ is a prime number. Then $p=3$, $5$, $7$, $11$, $13$, or $19$. Moreover, let ${\mathcal J}$ denote the set of ${\mathbb Z}_p$-invariant, $\omega$-compatible almost complex structures on $M$ which are integrable near the fixed point set of the ${\mathbb Z}_p$-action. Then for any generic $J\in{\mathcal J}$, there is a ${\mathbb Z}_p$-invariant $J$-holomorphic curve $C$ in $M$ which contains all $3$ fixed points of the ${\mathbb Z}_p$-action and is embedded in the complement of the fixed point set. Further information about $C$ as well as the local representations of the ${\mathbb Z}_p$-action at the fixed point set are stated below:
\begin{itemize}
\item [{(1)}] For $p=3$, $C$ is of genus $25$, has a nodal singularity at each of the $3$ fixed points, and 
$c_1(K)=\frac{1}{2}C$. The rotation numbers at each of the $3$ fixed points is $(1,2)$ {\em(}for any generator 
of ${\mathbb Z}_p${\em)}. 
\item [{(2)}] For $p=5$, $C$ is of genus $23$, has a nodal singularity at one of the fixed points and has two embedded local branches with a tangency of order $2$ at each of the other two fixed points, and 
$c_1(K)=\frac{1}{2}C$. For some generator of ${\mathbb Z}_p$, the rotation numbers is $(1,4)$ at the nodal singularity and are $(4,3)$ and $(1,2)$ respectively at the other two fixed points. 
\item [{(3)}] For $p=7$, there are five subcases: 
\begin{itemize}
\item [{(i)}] $C$ is embedded, of genus $10$, and $c_1(K)=C$. The rotation numbers at the $3$ fixed points are $(1,3)$, $(6,2)$, and $(4,5)$ for some generator of ${\mathbb Z}_p$.
\item [{(ii)}] $C$ is of genus $27$, has a nodal singularity at one of the fixed points and is embedded near the other two fixed points, and $c_1(K)=\frac{1}{2}C$. For some generator of ${\mathbb Z}_p$, the rotation numbers is $(1,6)$ at the nodal singularity and are $(6,5)$ and $(1,2)$ respectively at the other two fixed points.
\item [{(iii)}] $C$ is of genus $23$, has a simple cusp singularity at one of the fixed points, a nodal singularity at another, and a reducible singularity at the third fixed point, where one of the local branches is embedded and the other local branch contains a simple cusp, with the intersection number of the two local branches equaling $2$, 
and $c_1(K)=\frac{1}{2}C$. For some generator of ${\mathbb Z}_p$, the rotation numbers is $(2,3)$ at the simple cusp, $(2,6)$ at the nodal singularity, and $(4,6)$ at the reducible singularity.
\item [{(iv)}] $C$ is of genus $19$, with $c_1(K)=\frac{1}{2}C$, and at one of the fixed points, $C$ has three embedded local branches, two of which are tangent of order $2$ intersecting the third local branch transversely,
while at another fixed point, $C$ has two embedded local branches which are tangent of order $2$, and at the last fixed point, $C$ has a cuspidal singularity whose link is a $(3,4)$-torus knot. For some generator of ${\mathbb Z}_p$, the rotation numbers are $(1,4)$, $(6,3)$, and $(3,4)$ respectively at the first, second, and third fixed point.
\item [{(v)}] $C$ is of genus $19$, with $c_1(K)=\frac{1}{2}C$, and at each of the $3$ fixed points, $C$ has two embedded local branches which are tangent of order $3$. For some generator of ${\mathbb Z}_p$, the rotation numbers are $(1,3)$, $(6,2)$, and $(4,5)$ respectively at the $3$ fixed points. 
\end{itemize}
\item [{(4)}] For $p=11$, there are two subcases: 
\begin{itemize}
\item [{(i)}] $C$ is of genus $5$, has a simple cusp singularity at one of the fixed points and is 
embedded near the other two fixed points, with $c_1(K)=\frac{3}{2}C$. The rotation numbers at the $3$ fixed points are $(2,3)$, $(2,10)$, and $(3,1)$ respectively for some generator of ${\mathbb Z}_p$. 
\item [{(ii)}] $C$ is of genus $15$, with $c_1(K)=\frac{1}{2}C$, and is embedded at one of the fixed points, has two embedded local branches at another, which are tangent of order $5$, and has two tangent local branches at the third fixed point, where each local branch contains a simple cusp singularity. For some generator of ${\mathbb Z}_p$, the rotation numbers are $(1,3)$, $(10,2)$, and $(8,9)$ respectively at the first, second, and third fixed point.
\end{itemize}
\item [{(5)}] For $p=13$, there are two subcases: 
\begin{itemize}
\item [{(i)}] $C$ is embedded, of genus $6$,  with $c_1(K)=\frac{3}{2}C$. The rotation numbers at the $3$ fixed points are $(1,6)$, $(1,8)$ and $(6,5)$ for some generator of ${\mathbb Z}_p$.
\item [{(ii)}] $C$ is of genus $19$, has a cuspidal singularity of $\delta$-invariant $3$ at each of the fixed points, 
with $c_1(K)=\frac{1}{2}C$. The rotation numbers at the $3$ fixed points are $(3,4)$, $(10,1)$, and $(9,12)$ for some generator of ${\mathbb Z}_p$.
\end{itemize}
\item[{(6)}] For $p=19$, $C$ is embedded, of genus $28$, with $c_1(K)=\frac{1}{2}C$. The rotation numbers at the $3$ fixed points are $(1,12)$, $(18,11)$, and $(7,8)$ respectively for some generator of ${\mathbb Z}_p$.
\end{itemize}

title: Remark
body_md:
(1) Primary examples of a symplectic ${\mathbb Q}$-homology ${\mathbb C}{\mathbb P}^2$ with positive canonical class, which are also the only known examples, are the fake projective planes, which are completely classified by Prasad and Yeung \cite{PY} following Yau's solution of Calabi's conjecture \cite{Y} (see also Cartwright and Steger \cite{CS} for the computer-assisted group theoretic computations). Based on their classification of the fake projective planes, Keum \cite{Keum2} further classified the quotient space and local representations of a finite automorphism group of a fake projective plane. In particular, it was shown that the prime order automorphisms are of order either $3$ or $7$. Regarding symplectic ${\mathbb Q}$-homology ${\mathbb C}{\mathbb P}^2$ with positive canonical class as the symplectic analog of the fake projective planes, Theorem 1.3 suggests that potentially, there are symplectic ${\mathbb Z}_p$-actions on a symplectic fake projective plane which are not algebraic.  

More concretely, note that in Cases (2), (4), (5), and (6) of Theorem 1.3, the order $p\neq 3$ or $7$. On the other hand, concerning the action near the fixed points, a symplectic ${\mathbb Z}_p$-action in Theorem 1.3 is said of {\bf holomorphic} local representations if its local representations are the same as the local representations of a ${\mathbb Z}_p$-automorphism of a fake projective plane. A symplectic ${\mathbb Z}_p$-action is said of {\bf linear} local representations if its local representations are the same as that of a linear 
${\mathbb Z}_p$-action on ${\mathbb C}{\mathbb P}^2$. One can check easily that holomorphic local representations are also linear. With this understood, in Theorem 1.3 the symplectic ${\mathbb Z}_p$-action has holomorphic local representations in Cases (1), (3)(i), and (3)(v). (In fact, the local representations in Cases (3)(i) and (3)(v) are the same; the difference lies in the invariant curves. In all other cases, the symplectic ${\mathbb Z}_p$-actions differ in either the order $p$ or the local representations.) Moreover, it has linear local representations (but not holomorphic) in Cases (2), (3)(ii), (3)(iv), (4)(ii), (5)(ii), and (6). In the remaining cases, i.e., Cases (3)(iii), (4)(i), and (5)(i), the symplectic ${\mathbb Z}_p$-action has exotic (i.e., nonlinear) local representations. We remark that none of the symplectic ${\mathbb Z}_p$-actions in Theorem 1.3 can be further eliminated by the existing obstructions (however, it is very likely that there are cases that can be ruled out as a consequence of Theorem 1.1). 

It follows easily that a ${\mathbb Z}_p$-automorphism of a fake projective plane, if regarded as a symplectic 
${\mathbb Z}_p$-action on a ${\mathbb Q}$-homology ${\mathbb C}{\mathbb P}^2$, must belong to one of the following three cases:  (1), (3)(i), or (3)(v). It is clear that any ${\mathbb Z}_3$-automorphism of a fake projective plane belongs to the unique Case (1), although it is interesting to note that, according to the computations in \cite{CS}, there are at least six fake projective planes which admits a ${\mathbb Z}_3$-automorphism (cf. \cite{PY1}). However, for the case of $p=7$, the situation is less straightforward. There is a ${\mathbb Z}_7$-automorphism of a fake projective plane which could belong to either Case (3)(i) or (3)(v), and there is also a 
${\mathbb Z}_7$-automorphism which only belongs to Case (3)(v). See Theorem 3.9 for more details. 

(2) One crucial assertion in Theorem 1.3 is that in all the cases of the group action, the invariant curve $C$ contains all $3$ fixed points of the action, and is embedded in the complement of the fixed-point set. This has the following important consequence: in the minimal resolution $X$ of the symplectic quotient orbifold, the proper transform of the quotient curve $C/{\mathbb Z}_p$ connects the exceptional divisors from the resolution of the $3$ quotient singularities to form a {\it connected} symplectic divisor $D$ with normal crossings. With this understood, the $12$ weighted graphs in Figure 1 are the corresponding plumbing graphs for the $12$ cases of group actions listed in Theorem 1.3, where the graphs are labeled as either $\Gamma_p$ or $\Gamma_{p,i}$, with $p$ being the order of the group action, and in the latter case $\Gamma_{p,i}$, with $i$ indicating the subcase of the group actions of order $p$ in the listing in Theorem 1.3, e.g., $\Gamma_{7,5}$ is the plumbing graph corresponding to the group action in Case (3)(v). 

By the work of Li and Mak \cite{LM}, after changing the symplectic structure via a deformation if necessary, a regular neighborhood of the symplectic divisor $D$, which is modeled by the symplectic plumbing $P_\Gamma$ according to the weighted graph $\Gamma$, has a concave contact boundary 
$(Y_\Gamma, \xi_{LM})$. This allows us to decompose the minimal resolution $X$ as a union of two pieces, one is the regular neighborhood of the symplectic divisor $D$, a standard piece, and the other is its complement in $X$, which is a strong symplectic filling of the contact plumbed manifold 
$(Y_\Gamma, \xi_{LM})$. This canonical decomposition of the minimal resolution of the quotient 
orbifold established a fundamental connection between the group actions under consideration and the symplectic fillings of the $12$ plumbed manifolds $(Y_\Gamma, \xi_{LM})$, which plays the key role in Theorem 1.1. Indeed, Theorem 1.1(2) follows readily from this decomposition, and Theorem 1.1(1) follows from a corresponding reverse-engineering procedure.

title: Lemma
body_md:
Fixing any generator $g\in G$ and any fixed point $q$, there is a pair of integers $0<a<b<p$ such that 
$(a,b)$ is the rotation numbers at $q$, and the rotation numbers at the other two fixed points are given in the following four cases:
\begin{itemize}
\item [{(i)}] $(p-a,b-a)$ and $(p-b,p+a-b)$. 
\item [{(ii)}] $(a, p+a-b)$ and $(p-b, p+a-b)$.
\item [{(iii)}] $(p-a,b-a)$ and $(b, b-a)$.
\item [{(iv)}] $(a, p+a-b)$ and $(b, b-a)$.
\end{itemize}
In particular, we observe that if $(a,b)=(1,2)$, then (1) there is a fixed point $\tilde{q}\neq q$, such that for any
rotation numbers $(\tilde{a},\tilde{b})$ at $\tilde{q}$, $\tilde{a}+\tilde{b}=p$, and (2) with respect to either $g$ or 
$g^{-1}$, $(1,2)$ is also the rotation numbers at a fixed point $q^\prime \neq q$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $(a_i,b_i)$, for $i=1,2,3$, be the rotation numbers at the $3$ fixed points, where without loss of generality, we assume $(a_1,b_1)=(a,b)$. Then by a theorem of Edmonds and Ewing (cf. \cite{EE}), up to a simultaneous change of sign, the rotation numbers at the other two fixed points are given by the rotation numbers of a corresponding linear $G$-action on ${\mathbb C}{\mathbb P}^2$, which in particular implies that $a\neq b$. If we assume $a<b$ without loss of generality, then the rotation numbers of the linear action are $(p-a,b-a)$ and $(p-b,p+a-b)$ respectively at the other
two fixed points. Consequently, either $(a_2,b_2)$ or $(p-a_2,p-b_2)$ equals $(p-a,b-a)$ and  either $(a_3,b_3)$ or $(p-a_3,p-b_3)$ equals $(p-b,p+a-b)$ respectively. The lemma follows immediately.

title: Lemma
body_md:
For any $J\in{\mathcal J}$, there is a finite set of irreducible $J$-holomorphic curves $\{C_i\}$ with multiplicities $\{n_i\}$,
such that $c_1(2K)=\sum_i n_i C_i$. Furthermore, the set $\cup_i C_i$ is invariant under the $G$-action and the $3$ fixed points of $G$ are all contained in $\cup_i C_i$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $d(2K)$ be the virtual dimension of the $G$-invariant Seiberg-Witten moduli space associated to
the $G$-equivariant complex line bundle $2K$. Then the key to the proof is to show $d(2K)\geq 0$, 
as explained in \cite{C}, Section 4. The point is that, under this condition, a wall-crossing argument implies that the corresponding $G$-equivariant Seiberg-Witten invariant is nonzero in the Taubes chamber, and as a consequence, $c_1(2K)=\sum_i n_i C_i$ for a finite set of $J$-holomorphic curves $C_i$ such that $\cup_i C_i$ is invariant under the $G$-action and contains any fixed point $q$ whose rotation numbers $(a,b)$ obeys $2(a+b)\neq 0\pmod{p}$, which is equivalent to $a+b \neq 0\pmod{p}$ as $p$ is odd. 

We need to explain why the $J$-holomorphic curves $C_i$ can be so chosen such that $\cup_i C_i$ contains all
$3$ fixed points. To this end, we need to recall the calculation of $d(2K)$. Let $(a_i,b_i)$, for $i=1,2,3$, be the rotation numbers at the $3$ fixed points. Then $d(2K)$ is given by the following formula: 
$$
d(2K)=\frac{1}{p}(c_1(2K)^2- c_1(2K)\cdot c_1(K)+\sum_{i=1}^3 \sum_{x=1}^{p-1} 
\frac{2(\mu_p^{-2(a_i+b_i)x}-1)}{(1-\mu_p^{-a_ix})(1-\mu_p^{-b_ix})}),
$$
where $\mu_p:=\exp(2\pi i/p)$. See \cite{C1}, Appendix A, also Lemma 3.3 in \cite{C0}. In the present case,
with $c_1(K)^2=9$, it was shown in \cite{C}, Section 4, that $d(2K)$ is given by the following formula
$$
d(2K)=\frac{1}{p}(18+6(p-1)-2\sum_{i=1}^3 (\delta(a_i+b_i,b_i)+\delta (b_i,a_i))),
$$
where for any $0\leq c\leq p$, $0<d<p$, $\delta(c,d)$ is the unique solution to $c-d\delta=0 \pmod{p}$ where
$0\leq \delta<p$ (see Lemma 4.4 in \cite{C}). 

With the preceding understood, in order to evaluate $d(2K)$, we assume without loss of generality that
$(a_1,b_1)=(a,b)$, and $(a_2,b_2)$ and $(a_3,b_3)$ are given as in Lemma 2.1. Furthermore, for an illustration
we assume we are in case (i). Then we observe the following: 
\begin{itemize}
\item [{(1)}] $b-a \delta(b_1,a_1)=0 \pmod{p}$.
\item [{(2)}] $b-a-(p-a) \delta(b_2,a_2)= 0\pmod{p}$. 
\item [{(3)}] $p+a-b-(p-b) \delta (b_3,a_3)=0 \pmod{p}$. 
\item [{(4)}] $a+b- b\delta(a_1+b_1, b_1)=0 \pmod{p}$.
\item [{(5)}] $p-2a+b-(b-a) \delta(a_2+b_2, b_2)=0 \pmod{p}$. 
\item [{(6)}] $2p+a-2b -(p+a-b)\delta (a_3+b_3,b_3)=0 \pmod{p}$.
\end{itemize}
Note that (1) and (2) implies $\delta(b_1,a_1)+\delta(b_2,a_2)=1\pmod{p}$, (5) and (6) implies that
$\delta(a_2+b_2,b_2)+\delta(a_3+b_3,b_3)=3 \pmod{p}$, and finally,  (3) and (4) implies that 
$\delta(a_1+b_1,b_1)+\delta(b_3,a_3)=2 \pmod{p}$. It follows easily that 
$$
\delta(b_1,a_1)+\delta(b_2,a_2)=p+1,
$$
$$
\delta(a_2+b_2,b_2)+\delta(a_3+b_3,b_3)=\left \{\begin{array}{ll} 
0 & \mbox{ if $a_i+b_i=p$ for both $i=2,3$} \\
3 & \mbox{ if exactly for one of $i=2,3$, $a_i+b_i=p$ } \\
p+3 & \mbox{ if $a_i+b_i\neq 0 \pmod{p}$ for $i=2,3$ }\\
\end{array} \right. 
$$
and 
$$
\delta(a_1+b_1,b_1)+\delta(b_3,a_3)=\left \{\begin{array}{ll} 
2 & \mbox{ if $a_1+b_1=p$}\\
p+2 & \mbox{ if $a_1+b_1\neq 0\pmod{p}$.}
\end{array} \right. 
$$
We further observe that if $a_i+b_i=p$ for both $i=2,3$, then $b-2a=0\pmod{p}$ and $a-2b=0\pmod{p}$, which
implies that $p=3$ must be true, and $a_1+b_1=p$ as well. On the other hand, if $a_1+b_1=p$ and for one of 
$i=2,3$, $a_i+b_i=p$, $p=3$ must also be true, and $a_i+b_i=p$ for the other $i=2,3$ as well. 
With this understood, if we let $k$ be the number of fixed points whose rotation numbers $(a_i,b_i)$
obeys $a_i+b_i=p$, then either $k=3$ with $p=3$, or $k\leq 1$. It follows easily that when $k=3$, we have
$\sum_{i=1}^3 (\delta(a_i+b_i,b_i)+\delta (b_i,a_i))=p+3$, and as a result 
$$
d(2K)=\frac{1}{p}(18+6(p-1)-2(p+3))=\frac{1}{p}(6+4p)=6=2k,
$$
as in this case we have $p=3$. If $k=1$, we have $\sum_{i=1}^3 (\delta(a_i+b_i,b_i)+\delta (b_i,a_i))=2p+6$,
and 
$$
d(2K)=\frac{1}{p}(18+6(p-1)-2(2p+6))=2=2k,
$$
and if $k=0$, we have $\sum_{i=1}^3 (\delta(a_i+b_i,b_i)+\delta (b_i,a_i))=3p+6$, and $d(2K)=0$. 

With the preceding understood, we note that if $d(2K)=2k>0$, then we can arrange so that $\cup_i C_i$ contains
any chosen set of $k$ distinct points in $M$ (cf. Taubes \cite{T}). So when $k>0$, we may simply choose the $k$ distinct points to be the $k$ fixed points whose rotation numbers $(a_i,b_i)$ obeys $a_i+b_i=p$. This shows that we can always arrange so that $\cup_i C_i$ contains all $3$ fixed points. 

For the other cases, i.e., (ii)-(iv), the proof is identical. We simply make the following observation: if we change 
$c,d$ to $p-c,p-d$, the number $\delta(c,d)$ remains unchanged, i.e., $\delta(c,d)=\delta(p-c,p-d)$, and furthermore,
$a_i+b_i=p$ if and only if $(p-a_i)+(p-b_i)=p$.

title: Lemma
body_md: Let $J\in{\mathcal J}$ be generic. Then each $J$-holomorphic curve $C\in\{C_i\}$, where $c_1(2K)=\sum_i n_i C_i$, must be invariant under the $G$-action.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose to the contrary that there is a $C\in\{C_i\}$ which is not invariant under the $G$-action. Then 
$\{g\cdot C|g\in G\}$ is a set of $p=|G|$ distinct $J$-holomorphic curves, which is a subset of $\{C_i\}$. 
It follows easily that the degree $d$ of $C$ is at most $2$.

On the other hand, let $f: \Sigma\rightarrow M$ be a $J$-holomorphic parametrization of $C$, and let $\pi: M\rightarrow M/G$ be the quotient map. Then $\pi\circ f: \Sigma\rightarrow M/G$ is a $J$-holomorphic parametrization of $\pi(C)$ because $C$ is not $G$-invariant and the order $p=|G|$ is prime. 
Let $g_\Sigma$ be the genus of $\Sigma$. Then the complex virtual dimension $d_C$ of the moduli space 
of $J$-holomorphic curves in the orbifold $M/G$ that contains $\pi(C)$ is given by
$$
d_C=c_1(T(M/G))\cdot \pi(C)+(g_\Sigma-1)=c_1(TM)\cdot C+(g_\Sigma-1)=-3d+ (g_\Sigma-1).
$$
(See \cite{CR}, Proposition 3.2.5). Since $J\in{\mathcal J}$ is generic, one has $d_C\geq 0$. On the other hand, by the adjunction inequality, we have $g_\Sigma\leq \frac{1}{2}(C\cdot C+c_1(K)\cdot C+2)=\frac{1}{2}(d^2+3d+2)$. Then $d_C\geq 0$ implies $d\geq 3$, which is a contradiction to $d\leq 2$ we obtained earlier.

title: Lemma
body_md:
Let $J\in{\mathcal J}$ be generic. Then each $J$-holomorphic curve $C\in\{C_i\}$, where $c_1(2K)=\sum_i n_i C_i$, must
be non-spherical, i.e., $C$ cannot be parametrized by a $J$-holomorphic map from ${\mathbb S}^2$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Assume to the contrary that there is a $C\in\{C_i\}$ which is parametrized by a $J$-holomorphic map 
$f: {\mathbb S}^2\rightarrow M$. By Lemma 2.3, $C$ is invariant under the $G$-action, which implies that there is an induced $G$-action on the domain ${\mathbb S}^2$, with respect to which $f$ is $G$-equivariant. Let $x,\tilde{x}\in {\mathbb S}^2$ be the two fixed points and let $q=f(x)$, $\tilde{q}=f(\tilde{x})$ be the corresponding fixed points in $M$. Furthermore, let

$\tilde{g}:=g^{-1}\in G$, which acts on ${\mathbb S}^2$ as a rotation of angle $2\pi/p$ at the fixed point $\tilde{x}$.

With the preceding understood, the complex virtual dimension $d_C$ for the component of the moduli space of 
orbifold $J$-holomorphic curves in the quotient orbifold $M/G$ that contains the curve $C/G$ is given by the following formula
$$
d_C=\frac{c_1(TM)\cdot C}{p}+1-\frac{a+b}{p}-\frac{\tilde{a}+\tilde{b}}{p}=1-\frac{3d+a+b+\tilde{a}+\tilde{b}}{p}, 
$$
where $d>0$ is the degree of $C$. (See \cite{C0}, Lemma 1.10, also \cite{CR}, Lemma 3.2.4).
Note that since $J\in{\mathcal J}$ is generic, one has $d_C\geq 0$. 

We shall derive a contradiction by examining the values of $(\tilde{a},\tilde{b})$ using Lemma 2.1. First,
if $\tilde{q}=q$, then $(\tilde{a},\tilde{b})=(p-a,p-b)$, which implies $d_C<0$, a contradiction. Next, suppose 
the rotation numbers at $\tilde{q}$ with respect to the generator $g$ is $(a_2,b_2)$ in Lemma 2.1. Then 
$(\tilde{a},\tilde{b})$ equals either $(p-a, b-a)$ or $(a, p+a-b)$. In either case $d_C<0$, also a contradiction. Lastly, assume the rotation numbers at $\tilde{q}$ with respect to the generator $g$ is $(a_3,b_3)$ in Lemma 2.1. Then 
$(\tilde{a},\tilde{b})$ equals either $(p-b, p+a-b)$ or $(b, b-a)$. In the former case, $d_C<0$, and in the latter,
$d_C=\frac{1}{p}(p-3d-3b)\geq 0$, which implies that $p=3d+3b$ as $d_C\in{\mathbb Z}$. But this contradicts the assumption that $p$ is prime, as $d>0$ and $b>0$. This finishes the proof of the lemma.

title: Lemma
body_md: Let $J\in{\mathcal J}$ be generic. If there is a $C\in \{C_i\}$ of degree $d$ such that $d\leq 3$, then $7\leq p\leq 13$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
To show $p\geq 7$,  the key observation is that for each $j=1,2,\cdots,k$, $m_{j,1}\neq m_{j,2}$, so that $m_{j,1}+m_{j,2}\geq 3$ (see Lemma 2.1). On the other hand, $g_\Sigma\leq \frac{1}{2}(d^2+3d+2)$ by the adjunction inequality, so that 
$g_{|\Sigma/G|}-1\leq \frac{1}{2p}(d^2+3d)-k (\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2p})$. It follows easily that
$$
d_C\leq \frac{d^2-3d}{2p}+k(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{5}{2p}). 
$$
With the assumption $d\leq 3$, and under the condition $p\leq 5$, we see immediately that $d_C\geq 0$ implies
that $d=3$ and $p=5$ must be true. Moreover, $m_{j,1}+m_{j,2}=3$, i.e., $(m_{j,1},m_{j,2})=(1,2)$, must be
true for each of the fixed point $f(z_j)\in C$. However, with $p=5$, this contradicts Lemma 2.1.  Hence $p\geq 7$. 

On the other hand, assume to the contrary that $p\geq 17$. Then by Lemma 2.5, $d^2+3d+3\geq p$, which implies that $d=3$ must be true, and $p=17$ or $19$. Furthermore, note that $d^2+3d+3<2p$, so that $2-2g_\Sigma-k=-p$ must be the only possibility in Lemma 2.5. Note that $2-2g_{|\Sigma/G|}-k=-1$, which implies that $k=3$ and $g_{|\Sigma/G|}=0$ as $k\geq 2$. In what follows, we shall rule out $p=17$ or $19$ by a case by case analysis. 

Consider first the case of $p=19$. From $2-2g_\Sigma-k=-p$ where $k=3$, it follows easily that
$g_\Sigma=9$, which, with $d=3$, implies that $C$ either has a cuspidal singularity of $\delta$-invariant $1$ (i.e., a simple cusp) at a fixed point or a nodal singularity at a fixed point, say $q_1$. In the former case, the rotation numbers $(m_{1,1},m_{1,2})$ at $q_1$ must be $(2,3)$, while the rotation numbers at the other two fixed
points $q_2,q_3$ must take the form of $(1,m_2)$ and $(1,m_3)$, as $C$ is embedded near $q_2,q_3$. With this understood, we note that
$$
d_C=-\frac{3d}{p}+ (g_{|\Sigma/G|}-1)+3-\sum_{j=1}^3 \frac{m_{j,1}+m_{j,2}}{p}
=\frac{1}{19}(22-m_2-m_3).
$$
With both $m_2,m_3\geq 2$, and $d_C\geq 0$ and $d_C\in{\mathbb Z}$, it follows easily that $m_2+m_3=22$. 
On the other hand, we apply Lemma 2.1 with $(a_1,b_1)=(a,b)=(2,3)$, we see the rotation numbers at the other two fixed points are $(a_2,b_2)=(17, 1)$ or $(2, 18)$, $(a_3,b_3)=(16, 18)$ or $(3, 1)$. It follows that $(1,m_2)$
is either $(1,9)$ or $(1,17)$, and $(1,m_3)$ is either $(1,3)$ or $(1,13)$. Now with $m_2+m_3=22$, we must have
$(1,m_2)=(1,9)$ and $(1,m_3)=(1,13)$. However, one can check easily that the Global Quotient Criterion fails here.  Hence the former case is eliminated. 

For the latter case where there is a nodal singularity at $q_1$, the rotation numbers $(m_{j,1},m_{j,2})$ takes the form of $(1,m_1)$ and $(1,m_2)$ for the two local branches. As $k=3$, there is another fixed point contained in $C$, where rotation numbers $(m_{j,1},m_{j,2})$ takes the form $(1,m_3)$. 
With this understood, observe that the fact that $d_C\geq 0$ and $d_C\in{\mathbb Z}$ implies that $m_1+m_2+m_3=26$. 
Now without loss of generality we assume $m_1\leq m_2$, Then observe the fact that $m_1m_2=1\pmod{19}$, $g_2=g_1^{m_2}$, which implies that $g_3=g_1^{-1-m_2}$. To proceed further, note that at the fixed points $q_2,q_3$, the rotation numbers with respect to $g_1\in G$ are $(18, m_1-1)$ or $(1,20-m_1)$ and 
$(19-m_1, 20-m_1)$ or $(m_1,m_1-1)$. Then $g_3=g_1^{-1-m_2}$ implies that $(1,m_3)$ must be one of the following: $(18-m_2, 19+m_1-m_2)$, $(1+m_2, m_2-m_1)$, $(1+m_1, 19+m_1-m_2)$, or $(18-m_1, m_2-m_1)$,
where $1<m_1<m_2$. One can check easily that any of the above choices for $(1,m_3)$ either contradicts 
$m_1 m_2=1\pmod{19}$, or $m_1+m_2+m_3=26$, or both. Hence the latter case is also eliminated. This completes the discussion for $p=19$. 

For $p=17$, $2-2g_\Sigma-k=-p$ with $k=3$ implies that $g_\Sigma=8$. With $d=3$, it follows easily
that $C$ is singular, either with (i) a cuspidal singularity of $\delta$-invariant $2$, or (ii) two simple cusp singularities, or (iii) one simple cusp singularity and one nodal singularity, all occurring at the fixed points. In case (i), the rotation numbers $(m_{j,1},m_{j,2})$ take the form of $(2,5)$, $(1,m_2)$, and $(1,m_3)$, where by a similar calculation with the virtual dimension $d_C$, $m_2+m_3=16$ must hold true. On the other hand, using Lemma 2.1, with 
$(a,b)=(2,5)$, one finds that $(1,m_2)$ is either $(1,7)$ or $(1,5)$, and $(1,m_3)$ is either $(1,4)$ or $(1,13)$. It is easy to see that none of the above choices yields $m_2+m_3=16$, hence (i) is ruled out. In case (ii), the rotation numbers $(m_{j,1},m_{j,2})$ take the form of $(2,3)$, $(2,3)$, and $(1,m_3)$. Using Lemma 2.1, one finds that this is not possible. Hence (ii) is also ruled out. Finally, consider case (iii). The rotation numbers $(m_{j,1},m_{j,2})$ take the form of $(1,m_1)$, $(1,m_2)$, and $(2,3)$, where the first two occur at the nodal point and the last one at the simple cusp singularity. With this understood, we note that $g_2=g_1^{m_2}$ and $g_3=g_1^{-1-m_2}$, which implies that $m_1m_2=1\pmod{17}$ and $(2,3)$ must be one of the following: $(16-m_2, 17+m_1-m_2)$, $(1+m_2, m_2-m_1)$, $(1+m_1, 17+m_1-m_2)$, or $(16-m_1, m_2-m_1)$, where $1<m_1<m_2$.
In fact, only $(2,3)=(16-m_1,m_2-m_1)$ is possible, but it is a contradiction to $m_1m_2=1\pmod{17}$. Thus (iii) is also eliminated, and consequently, $p\neq 17$. 

The proof of Lemma 2.6 is completed.

title: Lemma
body_md:
For any of the fixed point $q_i$, $i=1,2,3$, suppose $(m_{1},m_{2})$ is the rotation numbers at $q_i$ with respect to some generator $g\in G$. Then there exists a pair of non-negative integers $a_1,a_2$, with $a_1+a_2>0$ and obeying 
$$
(a_1+2)m_{1}+(a_2+2)m_{2}=0 \pmod{p},
$$
such that for any local $J$-holomorphic disk $D$ containing the fixed point $q_i$, the local intersection number
of $D$ and $C$ at $q_i$, denoted by $int_D(q_i)$,  is at least $a_1+a_2$, i.e., 
$$
int_D(q_i)\geq a_1+a_2.
$$
In particular, if $C$ is embedded near $q_i$, and let $(1,m)$, where $m>1$, be the rotation numbers at $q_i$, then $p>5$, and either $2+3m=p$, or $2+3m=2p$, or $3+2m=p$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: The proof of the lemma is identical to that of Lemma 1.6 in \cite{C}, where instead of having the canonical line bundle $K$ as in \cite{C}, we have $2K$ here.  We refer the reader to \cite{C} for details. Regarding the special case where $C$ is embedded near $q_i$, we note that $int_D(q_i)=1$ for a generic $D$. Thus $a_1+a_2=1$ must be true, i.e., either $a_1=0$ and $a_2=1$, or $a_1=1$ and $a_2=0$. The lemma follows immediately.

title: Lemma
body_md: Let $J\in{\mathcal J}$ be generic. Suppose in $c_1(2K)=\sum_i n_i C_i$ from Lemma 2.2, $\{C_i\}$ consists of a single component $C$ of degree $d=6$. Then $p\leq 19$, and $p\neq 17$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We shall divide $p=17$, or $p\geq 23$ into a few cases and rule out each of the cases using different strategies 
and arguments.

\vspace{2mm}

{\bf (1):} $p\geq 37$. We begin by observing that with $d=6$, $d^2+3d+3=57<2p$, so that 
$2-2g_\Sigma-k=-p$ is the only possibility in Lemma 2.5. As such, one has $g_{|\Sigma/G|}=0$ and $k=3$. Since $C$ contains all $3$ fixed points, it follows easily that $C$ has only cuspidal singularities. Furthermore, $p\geq 37$ implies that $g_\Sigma\geq 18$, so that by the adjunction inequality, the sum of the $\delta$-invariants of the singularities of $C$ can not exceed $10$. 

With the preceding understood, we observe that if the $\delta$-invariant of a singularity of $C$ is less than $6$, the multiplicity of the singularity must be either $2$ or $3$, which is prime. It follows, with $p\geq 37$, that its rotation numbers $(m_{j,1},m_{j,2})$ must equal the characteristic sequence $(\alpha,\beta_1)$, therefore it must be
one of the following: $(2,3),(2,5),(2,7),(2,9), (2,11), (3,4), (3,5)$. Applying Lemma 2.7 to any of these choices,
it is easy to check that except for the case of $(2,11)$ with $p=37$, the sum $a_1+a_2$ is always greater than the multiplicity of the singularity. By Lemma 2.7, the local intersection number $int_D(q_i)$ is greater than the 
multiplicity of the singularity for any local $J$-holomorphic disc $D$. But for a generic local embedded $J$-holomorphic disc $D$, $int_D(q_i)$ equals the multiplicity of the singularity, by which we arrive at a contradiction. 
On the other hand, the case of $(2,11)$ with $p=37$ can be ruled out as follows: with $p=37$ and $k=3$, one has
$g_\Sigma=18$, which implies by the genus formula that the sum of the $\delta$-invariants of the singularities of $C$ equals $10$. It follows easily that $C$ must have two singularities, each with characteristic sequence 
$(\alpha,\beta_1)=(2,11)$ and $\delta$-invariant equaling $5$, and at the third fixed point $C$ is embedded. In particular, the rotation numbers $(m_{j,1},m_{j,2})$ at two of the fixed points are both $(2,11)$, which violates Lemma 2.1, because if we start out in Lemma 2.1 with $(a,b)=(2,11)$, the other $(2,11)$ can not be realized as rotation numbers at any of the two remaining fixed points for any generator $g\in G$. It follows easily that, 
for $p\geq 37$, $C$ must have at most one cuspidal singularity with a $\delta$-invariant between $6$ and $10$. 

To proceed further, we observe that if $p\geq 47$, then $g_\Sigma\geq 23$, which implies that the $\delta$-invariant of the singularity is less than $6$ by the genus formula, unless $C$ is embedded with $g_\Sigma=28$. But in this case, $p=57$ which is not prime. Consequently, it remains to examine the cases $p=37, 41$ or $43$, where $C$ has a unique cuspidal singularity. 

Let $p=43$. In this case, the $\delta$-invariant of the singularity of $C$ equals $7$. There are several possibilities for the rotation numbers at the fixed point: $(2,15)$ or $(3,8)$ if the multiplicity of the singularity equals $2$ or $3$ which are prime. Both possibilities can be easily eliminated by Lemma 2.7 as we argued before. On the other hand, it is easy to see that the multiplicity is at most $4$, and when it is $4$, the multiplicity sequence of the singularity
is $(4,2,1,1)$. But this is not realizable, hence $p=43$ is ruled out. 

Let $p=41$.  In this case, the $\delta$-invariant equals $8$. The multiplicity of the singularity is at most $4$. It is easy to see that $3$ and $4$ can not be realized. With this understood, the rotation numbers must be $(2,17)$ with the multiplicity being $2$. But this case can be ruled out by Lemma 2.7. Hence $p=41$ is eliminated. 

Finally, let $p=37$.  In this case, the $\delta$-invariant equals $10$, and the multiplicity of the singularity is at most $5$. For the cases where the multiplicity is a prime number, the rotation numbers at the fixed point is either 
$(2, 21)$, or $(3,11)$, or $(5,6)$. If the multiplicity equals $4$, then it is easy to see that the multiplicity sequence of the singularity must be $(4,2,2,2,2, 1,1)$, from which we see that the characteristic sequence of the singularity must be $(4,6,11)$. But this is not possible because one can not have two $\beta_j$'s (i.e., $6$ and $11$) which are both
less than $p=37$. On the other hand, the case $(2,21)$ can be eliminated using Lemma 2.7. For the remaining 
$(3,11)$ and $(5,6)$, we note that $C$ is embedded near the other two fixed points. The corresponding rotation numbers $(1,m_2)$ and $(1,m_3)$ can be determined using Lemma 2.7, which must be either $(1,24)$ or $(1,17)$. One can check easily that for either $(3,11)$ or $(5,6)$, these rotation numbers are not possible by Lemma 2.1. This eliminates $p=37$, and the analysis of Case (1) is completed.

\vspace{2mm}

{\bf (2):} $p=23,29$ or $31$. First of all, we note that in Lemma 2.5, for $p=29$ or $31$, $2-2g_\Sigma-k=-p$ is still the only possibility, but for $p=23$, $2-2g_\Sigma-k=-2p$ is also possible. Moreover, in the latter case, one has
$k=4$ and $g_{|\Sigma/G|}=0$ instead. In particular, $k=4$ implies that one of the singularity of $C$ will not be
cuspidal, i.e., $C$ has two local branches at the singularity. 

Let $p=31$. Then $2-2g_\Sigma-k=-p$ with $k=3$ implies that $g_\Sigma=15$, from which it follows that the 
sum of the $\delta$-invariants of the singularities of $C$ equals $13$. With this understood, it suffices to examine the following $4$ different scenarios, (i)-(iv).

{\bf (i):} $C$ has a singularity with $\delta$-invariant less than $7$ but not equal to $4$ or $6$. It is easy to check that the following are the possible rotation numbers at the fixed point: $(2,3)$, $(2,5)$, $(2,7)$, $(2,11)$, $(3,4)$. All these possibilities can be eliminated using Lemma 2.7. 

{\bf (ii):} $C$ has a singularity with $\delta$-invariant $4$. It follows easily that, since (i) is not possible, $C$ must have another singularity with $\delta$-invariant $9$, and at the remaining fixed point, $C$ is embedded. Let us examine the singularity with $\delta$-invariant $9$ more closely. It is easy to see that the multiplicity of the singularity is at most $4$. For the case of multiplicity being $2$ or $3$, it is easy to see that the rotation numbers at the fixed point are $(2,19)$ and $(3,10)$ respectively. One can check easily that these possibilities can be ruled out by Lemma 2.7. So the multiplicity must be $4$. With this understood, it follows easily that the characteristic sequence of the singularity is either $(4,7)$ or $(4,6,9)$. The latter case can be ruled out by noting that there are two $\beta_j$'s (i.e., $6$ and $9$) which are both less than $p=31$. In the former case, the rotation numbers at the fixed point is $(4,7)$, which can be ruled out by Lemma 2.7. 

{\bf (iii):} $C$ has a singularity with $\delta$-invariant $6$. It is easy to see that $C$ must have one more singularity with $\delta$-invariant $7$. Regarding the singularity with $\delta$-invariant $6$, the possible rotation numbers at the fixed point are $(2,13)$, $(3,7)$, or $(4,5)$, where $(2,13)$, $(3,7)$ can be eliminated using Lemma 2.7. For the singularity with $\delta$-invariant $7$, we find that if the multiplicity of the singularity is $4$, then the multiplicity sequence must be $(4,2,1,1)$, which can not be realized. 
If the multiplicity is $2$ or $3$, then the rotation numbers at the corresponding fixed point must be $(2,15)$ and
$(3,8)$ respectively, where $(2,15)$ can be ruled out by Lemma 2.7. Now to see (iii) is not possible, we simply observe that $(4,5)$ and $(3,8)$ cannot be both realized as rotation numbers at two different fixed points by 
Lemma 2.1. 

{\bf (iv):} $C$ has a unique singularity with $\delta$-invariant $13$. It is easy to see that the multiplicity of the singularity is at most $5$. For the primes $2,3$ and $5$, the characteristic sequences are of the form $(\alpha,\beta_1)$. With this understood, $\alpha=5$ can not be realized as $\frac{1}{2}(\alpha-1)(\beta_1-1)=13$ has no solution $\beta_1\in{\mathbb Z}$. On the other hand, for $\alpha=2$ and $3$, $\beta_1=27$ and $14$ respectively. The corresponding rotation numbers at the fixed point are $(2,27)$ and $(3,14)$ respectively. If the multiplicity equals $4$, it follows easily that the multiplicity sequence must be $(4,2,2,2,2,2,2,2,1,1)$. The corresponding characteristic 
sequence is $(4,6,17)$. However, this is not possible because there are two $\beta_j$'s (i.e., $6$ and $17$) which are both less than $p=31$. To eliminate $(2,27)$ and $(3,14)$, we note that $C$ is embedded near the other two fixed points. The corresponding rotation numbers $(1,m_2)$ and $(1,m_3)$ can be determined using Lemma 2.7, which are either $(1,20)$ or $(1,14)$. One can check easily that for either $(2,27)$ or $(3,14)$, these rotation numbers are not possible by Lemma 2.1. Hence $p=31$ is eliminated. 

Let $p=29$. In this case, the sum of the $\delta$-invariants of the singularities of $C$ equals $14$. The argument is similar, in which we consider $3$ different scenarios, (i)-(iii). 

{\bf (i):} $C$ has a singularity with $\delta$-invariant less than $8$ but not equal to $4$. One can show easily that the following are the possible rotation numbers at the fixed point: $(2,3)$, $(2,5)$, $(2,7)$, $(2,11)$, $(2,13)$, $(2,15)$, $(3,4)$, $(3,7)$, $(3,8)$, $(4,5)$. All these possibilities can be ruled out by Lemma 2.7. 

{\bf (ii):} $C$ has a singularity with $\delta$-invariant $4$. In this case, $C$ must have another singularity which has $\delta$-invariant $10$. Examining the singularity of $\delta$-invariant $10$, we note that the multiplicity of the singularity is at most $5$. For the cases of prime numbers, i.e., $2$, $3$, and $5$, the corresponding rotation numbers at the fixed point are $(2,21)$, $(3,11)$, and $(5,6)$ respectively.  All these possibilities can be ruled out by Lemma 2.7. If the multiplicity equals $4$, then it is easy to see that the multiplicity sequence of the singularity must be $(4,2,2,2,2,1,1)$. Correspondingly, the characteristic sequence is $(4,6,11)$. But this can not be realized because there are two $\beta_j$'s (i.e., $6$ and $11$) which are both less than $p=29$. 

{\bf (iii):} $C$ has a unique singularity with $\delta$-invariant $14$. Again the multiplicity of the singularity is at most $5$. If the multiplicity equals $2$, then the characteristic sequence of the singularity must be $(2,29)$. But $p=29$, so this can not be realized. If the multiplicity equals $4$, then the multiplicity sequence of the singularity is either $(4,4,2,2,1,1)$ or $(4,2,2,2,2,2,2,2,2,1,1)$. Correspondingly, the characteristic sequence is either $(4,10,11)$ or $(4,6,19)$. But both can not be realized because there are two $\beta_j$'s which are both less than $p=29$. Finally, it is easy to see that with the $\delta$-invariant being $14$, the multiplicity can not be $3$, and if the multiplicity equals $5$, the rotation numbers at the fixed point must be $(5,8)$. To eliminate this case, we note that $C$ is embedded near the other two fixed points. The corresponding rotation numbers $(1,m_2)$ and $(1,m_3)$ can be determined using Lemma 2.7, which are either $(1,9)$ or $(1,13)$. One can check easily that these rotation numbers are not possible by Lemma 2.1. Hence the case of $p=29$ is eliminated. 

Finally, let $p=23$. There are two cases in Lemma 2.5: (a) $2-2g_\Sigma-k=-2p$, (b) $2-2g_\Sigma-k=-p$. In case (a), one has $2-2g_{|\Sigma/G|}-k=-2$. With $k\geq 3$, one must have $k=4$. In case (b), $k=3$ as we observed earlier. 

{\bf (a):} In this case, $g_\Sigma=22$, and as $k=4$, we may assume without loss of generality that $k_1=2$, and $k_2=k_3=1$. In particular, at the fixed points $q_2,q_3$, $C$ can have only cuspidal singularities. Furthermore, it is easy to see that the sum of the $\delta$-invariants of the singularities at $q_2,q_3$ is at most $5$. Using Lemma 2.7, one can verify easily that $C$ is singular at most one of $q_2,q_3$, and if so, the rotation numbers at the fixed point must be $(3,4)$. On the other hand, if $C$ is embedded near $q_2$ or $q_3$, the corresponding rotation numbers must be $(1,7)$ or $(1,10)$ by Lemma 2.7. Using Lemma 2.1, one can easily check that these are not possible (either $C$ is embedded near one of $q_2,q_3$, or both). Hence (a) is eliminated. 

{\bf (b):} In this case, $g_\Sigma=11$, and $C$ has only cuspidal singularities, with the sum of the 
$\delta$-invariants equaling $17$. We first consider the case where $C$ has a singularity which has a $\delta$-invariant less than $10$. The multiplicity of the singularity is easily seen to be at most $4$. Using Lemma 2.7, one can rule out the possibility of multiplicity being $2$. Furthermore, if the multiplicity equals $3$, then the rotation numbers at the fixed point must be one of the following: $(3,4)$, $(3,7)$, $(3,8)$, and $(3,10)$; the case of $(3,5)$ can be ruled out by Lemma 2.7. If the multiplicity equals $4$, then the characteristic sequence of the singularity is either $(4,5)$, $(4,7)$, or $(4,6,9)$, where the last two cases can not be realized (the case $(4,7)$ is ruled out by Lemma 2.7). It follows easily from the above analysis that for any singularity of $C$ with a $\delta$-invariant less than 
$10$, its $\delta$-invariant must be either $3$, $6$, $7$, or $9$, With these understood, it suffices to consider the following $4$ scenarios, (i)-(iv), and eliminate them one by one. 

{\bf (i):} $C$ has a singularity with $\delta$-invariant $11$. The multiplicity of the singularity is at most $5$, and we shall examine them one by one. For the case of primes, i.e., $2,3$ and $5$, the characteristic sequence is of the form $(\alpha,\beta_1)$, where $\frac{1}{2}(\alpha-1)(\beta_1-1)=11$. For $\alpha=2$, $\beta_1=23=p$, which is not possible because $(\alpha,\beta_1)$ is also the rotation numbers at the fixed point. If $\alpha=3$, 
$\beta_1=12$, which contradicts the fact that $gcd(\alpha,\beta_1)=1$. If $\alpha=5$, there is no solution 
$\beta_1\in{\mathbb Z}$ to $\frac{1}{2}(\alpha-1)(\beta_1-1)=11$, hence this is also not possible. Finally, we assume the multiplicity equals $4$. Then it follows easily that the characteristic sequence must be $(4,6,13)$, which is not possible because one can not have two $\beta_j$'s (i.e., $6$ and $13$) which are both less than $p=23$. 

{\bf (ii):} $C$ has a singularity with $\delta$-invariant $3$. We note that the rotation numbers at the fixed point is $(3,4)$. With this understood, we observe that there are two possibilities: either $C$ is singular at the remaining fixed points, each of $\delta$-invariant $7$, or $C$ is singular at one of the remaining fixed points with $\delta$-invariant $14$, and is embedded near the other remaining fixed point. The latter case can be ruled out as we did in case (a), while in the former case, the rotation numbers at the $3$ fixed points are $(3,4)$, $(3,8)$, $(3,8)$ (each with respect to some generator in $G$). One can eliminate this possibility by Lemma 2.1. 

{\bf (iii):} $C$ has a singularity of $\delta$-invariant $7$. The rotation numbers at the fixed point is $(3,8)$. We only need to examine the case where $C$ is singular at one of the remaining fixed points, with a $\delta$-invariant $10$, and is embedded near the other remaining fixed point, at which the rotation numbers is either $(1,7)$ or $(1,10)$ by Lemma 2.7. Using Lemma 2.1, one can easily show that if $(3,8)$ is the rotation numbers at one of the fixed points, $(1,7)$ or $(1,10)$ can never be realized as rotation numbers at any other fixed point. 

{\bf (iv):} $C$ has a unique singularity with $\delta$-invariant $17$. Note that $C$ is embedded near
the remaining two fixed points, so the corresponding rotation numbers must be either $(1,7)$ or $(1,10)$ 
by Lemma 2.7. This case can be ruled out as we did in case (a). This eliminates the case of $p=23$, and the analysis of Case (2) is completed.

\vspace{2mm}

{\bf (3):} $p=17$. We begin with some quick but useful observations: if $C$ is embedded near a fixed point, then by Lemma 2.7 the rotation numbers at the fixed point must be either $(1,5)$ or $(1,7)$. On the other hand, by Lemma 2.1, it is easy to see that the rotation numbers $(1,5)$ or $(1,7)$ can not be realized at two different fixed points
(even with respect to different generators of $G$). As a consequence, $C$ cannot be embedded near more than one fixed points. Secondly, it also follows from Lemma 2.7 that $C$ cannot have a cuspidal singularity with $\delta$-invariant $1$ or $2$ at any fixed point, and if the $\delta$-invariant equals $3$, the rotation numbers at the fixed point must be $(3,4)$. With this understood, we note that there are $3$ cases to consider: 
(a) $2-2g_\Sigma-k=-3p$, (b) $2-2g_\Sigma-k=-2p$, and (c) $2-2g_\Sigma-k=-p$. See Lemma 2.5.

{\bf (a):} $2-2g_\Sigma-k=-3p$. In this case, $k=3$ or $5$. If $k=3$, then $g_\Sigma=25$, and $C$ has only cuspidal singularities at the fixed points, with the sum of the $\delta$-invariants equaling $3$. By the previous observations, it follows easily that $C$ has to be embedded near two of the $3$ fixed points, which is not possible. If $k=5$, then $g_\Sigma=24$. It follows from the genus formula for $g_\Sigma$ and the fact that $C$ can not be embedded near two different fixed points that $C$ must have two local branches at two of the fixed points and is embedded near the third fixed point, e.g.  $k_1=k_2=2$ and $k_3=1$ without loss of generality. Furthermore, if a local branch at one of the fixed points, say $q_1$, is singular, then by the genus formula for $g_\Sigma$ the only possibility is that the local branch has a $\delta$-invariant $1$ cuspidal singularity while the other local branch is embedded with their tangent planes being transversal at $q_1$, and $C$ must be embedded at $q_3$. As a consequence, the rotation numbers at $q_1$ associated to the two local branches must be $(2,3)$ and $(1,12)$ respectively. With the rotation numbers at $q_3$ (near where $C$ is embedded) being $(1,5)$ or $(1,7)$, one can easily check that Lemma 2.1 is violated. 

Hence both local branches at both $q_1,q_2$ must be embedded. With this understood, note that the genus formula for $g_\Sigma$ implies that the two local branches at one of $q_1,q_2$, say $q_1$, must be tangent to each other at the fixed point. As a consequence, the two local branches must determine the same rotation numbers, of the form $(1,m)$, where $m$ is the local intersection number of the two branches. It then follows from the genus formula for $g_\Sigma$ that $m<4$ must be true. To eliminate this possibility, we shall use Lemma 2.7. To see this, observe that $int_D(q_1)=2$ for a generic $D$. On the other hand, Lemma 2.7 implies that
$$
(2+a_1)+(2+a_2)m=0 \pmod{17}
$$
for some non-negative integers $a_1,a_2$ such that $0<a_1+a_2\leq 2$. It follows easily that $m=5,7,8,15$ or $16$, which contradicts $m<4$. Hence (a) is eliminated. 

{\bf (b):} $2-2g_\Sigma-k=-2p$. In this case, $k=4$, $g_{|\Sigma/G|}=0$, and $g_\Sigma=16$. With $k=4$, we assume without loss of generality that $k_1=2$, and $k_2=k_3=1$. Let $C_{1,1}, C_{2,1}$ be the two local branches of $C$ at the fixed point $q_1$, let $\delta_{1,1}, \delta_{2,1}$ be the corresponding $\delta$-invariants of the singularities contained in $C_{1,1}, C_{2,1}$, and let $\delta_2,\delta_3$ be the $\delta$-invariants of the singularities of $C$ at the fixed points $q_2,q_3$. Then it follows easily from the genus formula for $g_\Sigma=16$ that
$$
C_{1,1}\cdot C_{2,1}+\delta_{1,1}+\delta_{2,1}+\delta_2+\delta_3=28-16=12.
$$
In particular, $\delta_{1,1},\delta_{2,1},\delta_2,\delta_3\leq 11$. With this understood, in Table 1 below we list the possible $\delta$-invariants and rotation numbers at $q_2,q_3$ 
(after applying Lemma 2.7); in particular, note that $\delta$-invariant $\neq 1,2,4,5$ and $8$.

\vspace{3mm}

\centerline{
\begin{tabular}{lllllll}
\hline \vline\hspace{1mm}
$\delta$-invariant $\leq 11$ & \vline \hspace{1mm} rotation numbers  \hspace{5.8mm} \vline \\
\hline \vline\hspace{1mm}
0 &  \vline \hspace{1mm} $(1,5)$ or $(1,7)$ \hspace{11.6mm} \vline \\ 
\hline \vline\hspace{1mm} 
3 &  \vline \hspace{1mm} $(3,4)$  \hspace{26.1mm} \vline\\
\hline \vline\hspace{1mm} 
6 &  \vline \hspace{1mm} $(2,13)$, $(3,7)$ or $(4,5)$ \vline\\
\hline \vline\hspace{1mm} 
7 &  \vline \hspace{1mm} $(2,15)$  \hspace{24.2mm} \vline\\
\hline \vline\hspace{1mm} 
9 &  \vline \hspace{1mm} $(4,7)$  \hspace{26.1mm} \vline\\
\hline \vline\hspace{1mm} 
10 &  \vline \hspace{1mm} $(5,6)$  \hspace{26.1mm} \vline\\ \hline
\end{tabular}
}
\vspace{2mm}

\centerline{Table 1: $\delta$-invariants and rotation numbers at $q_2,q_3$, in Case (3)(b) with $p=17$.
}

\vspace{2mm}

With the preceding understood, there are $4$ scenarios, (i)-(iv), to consider. 

{\bf (i):} Both $\delta_{1,1},\delta_{2,1}$ are nonzero. Let $(a_1,b_1)$, $(a_2,b_2)$ be the rotation numbers associated to the local branches $C_{1,1},C_{2,1}$, where we may assume that they coincide with the characteristic sequences of the singularities. There are two possibilities: if $C_{1,1},C_{2,1}$ have the same tangent plane at $q_1$, then $(a_1,b_1)=(a_2,b_2)$ must be true, and in this case, $C_{1,1}\cdot C_{2,1}$ equals the sum of the square of all the entries in the multiplicity sequence, and if $C_{1,1},C_{2,1}$ have transverse tangent planes at 
$q_1$, then $C_{1,1}\cdot C_{2,1}=a_1a_2$ (i.e., the product of the multiplicities). With this understood, we observe
that $C_{1,1}\cdot C_{2,1}+\delta_{1,1}+\delta_{2,1}\leq 9$, as $C$ cannot be embedded at both $q_2,q_3$. It follows immediately that the multiplicity of both singularities must be $2$ (i.e., $a_1=a_2=2$). Assume one of 
$\delta_{1,1},\delta_{2,1}$ equals $1$. Then if $C_{1,1},C_{2,1}$ have the same tangent plane, we must have both 
$\delta_{1,1}=\delta_{2,1}=1$, and $C_{1,1}\cdot C_{2,1}=2^2+1^2+1^2=6$. If $C_{1,1},C_{2,1}$ have 
transverse tangent planes, then it is easy to see that we must have $(a_1,b_1)=(2,3)$, $(a_2,b_2)=(2,7)$. It follows 
that in both cases, $\delta_2+\delta_3=12-8=4$, which is easily seen not possible by Table 1. If both $\delta_{1,1},\delta_{2,1}\geq 2$, then the only possibility is that $\delta_{1,1}=2,\delta_{2,1}=3$, and $C_{1,1},C_{2,1}$ have 
transverse tangent planes, because $C_{1,1}\cdot C_{2,1}\neq 5$ and $\delta_2+\delta_3\neq 4$. With this understood, the rotation numbers $(a_1,b_1)$, $(a_2,b_2)$ associated to the two local branches $C_{1,1},C_{2,1}$ must be $(2,5)$ and $(2,7)$ respectively, which contradicts the fact that $C_{1,1},C_{2,1}$ have transverse tangent planes. Hence (i) is eliminated.

{\bf (ii):} $\delta_{1,1}=\delta_{2,1}=0$ and $C_{1,1}\cdot C_{2,1}=1$. In this case, we have $\delta_2+\delta_3=11$,
which is easily seen not possible by Table 1.

{\bf (iii):} $\delta_{1,1}=\delta_{2,1}=0$ and $m=C_{1,1}\cdot C_{2,1}>1$. In this case, the rotation numbers $(1,m)$ at $q_1$ is subject to Lemma 2.7, which implies that $m=5,7,8,15$, or $16$, and on the other hand, 
$\delta_2+\delta_3=12-m$. It follows easily that $m=5$ is the only possibility, and according to Table 1, the rotation numbers at $q_2,q_3$ must be $(1,5)$ (or $(1,7)$) and $(2,15)$ respectively. But this violates Lemma 2.1, hence
(iii) is eliminated.

{\bf (iv):} $\delta_{1,1}>0$ but $\delta_{2,1}=0$. Note that $\delta_2+\delta_3\geq 3$, which implies by the genus formula that 
$\delta_{1,1}\leq 7$. Consequently, the rotation numbers at $q_1$ that is associated to the local branch $C_{1,1}$
must be of the form $(\alpha,\beta_1)$ where $(\alpha,\beta_1)$ is the characteristic sequence of the singularity, 
and the multiplicity $\alpha=2,3$ or $4$, with $C_{1,1}\cdot C_{2,1}=\beta_1$ if $C_{1,1}, C_{2,1}$ are tangent at $q_1$ and $C_{1,1}\cdot C_{2,1}=\alpha$ if otherwise. Moreover, $(\alpha,\beta_1)$ is subject to a constraint 
from Lemma 2.7, i.e., if for any non-negative integers $a_1,a_2$ with $a_1+a_2>0$ and 
$$
(2+a_1)\alpha +(2+a_2)\beta_1=0 \pmod{17},
$$
one always has $a_1+a_2>\alpha+1=int_D(q_1)$ (here $D$ is generic), then $(\alpha,\beta_1)$ can be eliminated. Finally, we point out that
the rotation numbers at $q_1$ that is associated to the local branch $C_{2,1}$ is of the form $(1,m)$ which can be
determined completely from $(\alpha,\beta_1)$ and the fact of whether $C_{1,1}, C_{2,1}$ are tangent at $q_1$ or not. With this understood, we obtain the following list of possible rotation numbers at the fixed points, where in each case the first two rotation numbers are associated with $C_{1,1}, C_{2,1}$ and the last two rotation numbers are at $q_2$, $q_3$ respectively:
\begin{itemize}
\item [{(1)}] $(2,3)$, $(1,12)$, $(1,5)$ (or $(1,7)$), $(4,7)$.
\item [{(2)}] $(2,3)$, $(1,12)$, $(3,4)$, $(2,13)$ (or $(3,7)$), $(4,5)$).
\item [{(3)}] $(2,7)$, $(1,10)$, $(1,5)$ (or $(1,7)$), $(2,15)$.
\item [{(4)}] $(3,4)$, $(1,5)$, $(1,5)$ (or $(1,7)$), $(2,13)$ (or $(3,7)$), $(4,5)$).
\item [{(5)}] $(3,4)$, $(1,5)$, $(3,4)$, $(3,4)$.
\item [{(6)}] $(3,5)$, $(1,13)$, $(1,5)$ (or $(1,7)$), $(3,4)$.
\item [{(7)}] $(3,7)$, $(1,15)$, $(1,5)$ (or $(1,7)$), $(3,4)$.
\item [{(8)}] $(2,15)$, $(1,16)$, $(1,5)$ (or $(1,7)$), $(3,4)$.
\end{itemize}
All these cases can be eliminated by Lemma 2.1. 

{\bf (c):} $2-2g_\Sigma-k=-p$. In this case, $k=3$, $g_{|\Sigma/G|}=0$, and $g_\Sigma=8$. Moreover, either $C$ has $17$ nodal singularities or $17$ simple cusp singularities in the complement of the fixed points and at most cuspidal singularities at each fixed point $q_i$ with the sum of the $\delta$-invariants equaling $3$, or $C$ has only cuspidal singularities with the sum of the $\delta$-invariants equaling $20$. The former case is actually not possible because $C$ will be embedded near two different fixed points. The latter case can be ruled out by the fact that $d_C<0$. To see this, recall that with $k=3$, $d=6$,
$$
d_C=-\frac{18}{p}+(g_{|\Sigma/G|}-1)+3-\sum_{j=1}^3 \frac{m_{j,1}+m_{j,2}}{p}.
$$
Now with $g_{|\Sigma/G|}=0$, $d_C\geq 0$ is equivalent to $\sum_{j=1}^3 (m_{j,1}+m_{j,2})\leq 16$. With this 
understood, $d_C<0$ follows easily from the following observations: (i) there is at least one 
singularity of $C$ with $\delta$-invariant less than $11$, as $C$ cannot be embedded near more than one fixed points, and for such a singularity, one can check that the corresponding rotation numbers 
$(m_{j,1},m_{j,2})$ always obeys $m_{j,1}+m_{j,2}\geq 7$, (ii) if $(m_{j,1},m_{j,2})$ is at a fixed point near where $C$ is embedded, then $m_{j,1}+m_{j,2}\geq 6$, and finally, (iii) by Lemma 2.1, $m_{j,1}+m_{j,2}\geq 4$ for any $j$. This completes the analysis of Case (3).

title: Lemma
body_md:
Let $Z$ be a symplectic $4$-orbifold with only isolated singularities, and let $S$ be an embedded, $2$-dimensional symplectic suborbifold in $Z$, containing singularities $x_1,x_2,\cdots,x_k$. Let $g$ be the genus of the underlying Riemann surface of $S$, let $n_i$ be the order of the isotropy group at $x_i$ and $(1,b_i)$, where $0<b_i<n_i$ and $gcd(n_i,b_i)=1$, be the rotation numbers at $x_i$ where $b_i$ is the weight of the local action in the normal direction of $S$, and let $e\in{\mathbb Q}$ be the Euler number (or equivalently, the first Chern number) of the orbifold normal bundle of $S$ in $Z$. 
Then there is an $e_0\in{\mathbb Z}$ such that $e=e_0+\sum_{i=1}^k \frac{b_i}{n_i}$. Moreover, let $U$ be a regular neighborhood of $S$ in $Z$ and let $\tilde{U}$ be the pre-image of $U$ under the minimal symplectic resolution $\pi: \tilde{Z}\rightarrow Z$. Then $\tilde{U}$ is diffeomorphic to a plumbing of symplectic surfaces according to the weighted graph in Figure 2(a), where the weights $e_{i,j}$ are determined from the continued fractions 
$-n_i/b_i=[e_{i,1},e_{i,2},\cdots,e_{i,s_i} ]$, for $i=1,2,\cdots,k$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $S$ is an embedded $2$-dimensional symplectic suborbifold in $Z$, its orbifold normal bundle is well-defined, which is naturally an orbifold complex line bundle. With this understood, by Lemma 3.6 in \cite{C00}, we have $e=e_0+\sum_{i=1}^k \frac{b_i}{n_i}$ for some $e_0\in{\mathbb Z}$. It follows easily that
the boundary of the regular neighborhood $U$ of $S$ in $Z$ is the Seifert manifold $M(g; -e_0-k, (n_1,n_1-b_1), \cdots, (n_k,n_k-b_k))$ (cf. \cite{N}). On the other hand, $M(g; -e_0-k, (n_1,n_1-b_1), \cdots, (n_k,n_k-b_k))$ is also the boundary of a plumbing according to the weighted graph in Figure 2(a) (e.g. see \cite{NR}, Theorem 5.1). The lemma follows immediately.

title: Lemma
body_md:
Consider a linear ${\mathbb Z}_p$-action on ${\mathbb C}^2$ for an odd prime $p$, with rotation numbers $(a,b)$ at the origin with respect to some generator $g\in{\mathbb Z}_p$, and let $B\subset {\mathbb C}^2$ be a $4$-ball centered at origin equipped with some ${\mathbb Z}_p$-invariant K\"{a}hler form. Let $\pi: \tilde{B}\rightarrow B$ be the complex blowing-up at the origin and denote by $E\subset \tilde{B}$ the exceptional $(-1)$-sphere. Note that the ${\mathbb Z}_p$-action lifts to a holomorphic ${\mathbb Z}_p$-action on $\tilde{B}$, which is symplectic with respect to some invariant symplectic form on $\tilde{B}$. Let $U:=\tilde{B}/{\mathbb Z}_p$ denote the corresponding symplectic $4$-orbifold.
\begin{itemize}
\item [{(1)}] Assume $a<b$. Then $U$ has $2$ isolated singularities, and its minimal symplectic resolution 
$\tilde{U}$ is diffeomorphic to a plumbing of symplectic surfaces according to the weighted graph in Figure 2(b), where $0<\tilde{a},\tilde{b}<p$ are determined as follows: let $s\in{\mathbb Z}$ such that $(b-a)s=1\pmod{p}$, then $\tilde{a}=as\pmod{p}$ and $\tilde{b}=-bs\pmod{p}$, and $-p/\tilde{a}=[e_{1,1},e_{1,2}, \cdots, e_{1,s_1}]$,  
$-p/\tilde{b}=[e_{2,1},e_{2,2}, \cdots, e_{2,s_2}]$ as continued fractions. 
\item [{(2)}] Assume $a=b=1$. Then $U$ is a smooth manifold with a symplectic structure such that the exceptional $(-1)$-sphere $E\subset \tilde{B}$ descends to an embedded symplectic $(-p)$-sphere in $U$. Moreover, for any embedded holomorphic disc $D\subset B$ through the origin, let $\tilde{D}$ be the proper transform in $\tilde{B}$. Then $\tilde{D}$ descends to an embedded symplectic disc in $U$ intersecting transversely and positively with the symplectic $(-p)$-sphere in $U$ at a single point. 
\end{itemize}

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $z_1,z_2$ be the complex coordinates on ${\mathbb C}^2$, where the action of $g\in{\mathbb Z}_p$ is given by $g\cdot (z_1,z_2)=(\mu_p^a z_1, \mu_p^b z_2)$,
$\mu_p:=\exp(2\pi i/p)$. Then the induced action of $g$ on the blowing-up $\tilde{B}$ is given by $g\cdot ((z_1,z_2), [z_1:z_2])=
((\mu_p^a z_1, \mu_p^b z_2),[\mu_p^a z_1:\mu_p^b z_2])$. 

First, assume $a<b$. Then the ${\mathbb Z}_p$-action on $\tilde{B}$ has $2$ isolated fixed points, both lying on the exceptional $(-1)$-sphere, i.e., $[1:0]$ and $[0:1]$ in $E$. Near the fixed point $[1:0]$, the local chart of  $\tilde{B}$ is given by $((z_1,z_2), [z_1:z_2])\rightarrow (z_1,z_2/z_1)$, which implies that the rotation numbers at $[1:0]$ is $(a,b-a)$ with respect to $g$. Similarly, the rotation numbers at the fixed point $[0:1]$ is $(b,p+a-b)$ with respect to $g$. With this understood, we apply Lemma 3.1 to the $2$-dimensional symplectic suborbifold $S:=E/{\mathbb Z}_p$ in the symplectic $4$-orbifold $U:=\tilde{B}/{\mathbb Z}_p$. It is easy to see that $S$ contains $2$ isolated singularities with rotation numbers $(1,b_1)$, $(1,b_2)$, where $b_1=\tilde{a}$, $b_2=\tilde{b}$. To finish up, we observe that 
$\tilde{a}+\tilde{b}=s(a-b)=-1 \pmod{p}$, which implies easily that $\tilde{a}+\tilde{b}=p-1$. On the other hand,
it is clear that the Euler number $e$ of the orbifold normal bundle of $E/{\mathbb Z}_p$ in $\tilde{B}/{\mathbb Z}_p$ is $-1/p$. It follows immediately that $e_0=-1$, and by Lemma 3.1, the minimal symplectic resolution $\tilde{U}$ is diffeomorphic to a plumbing of symplectic surfaces according to the weighted graph in Figure 2(b). 

Next, assume $a=b=1$. Then the ${\mathbb Z}_p$-action on $\tilde{B}$ fixes the exceptional $(-1)$-sphere $E$ and has no other fixed points. Consequently, the underlying space of the symplectic $4$-orbifold $U:=\tilde{B}/{\mathbb Z}_p$ is a smooth manifold, and according to \cite{C11}, one can de-singularize the orbifold symplectic structure on 
$U:=\tilde{B}/{\mathbb Z}_p$, so that $U$ becomes a symplectic $4$-manifold. Furthermore, the singular set $E/{\mathbb Z}_p$ in $U$ becomes an embedded symplectic $(-p)$-sphere in the symplectic $4$-manifold $U$. Other claims in part (2) follows from the construction in \cite{C11} easily as well. The proof of Lemma 3.2 is completed.
